fixes.explanation: That's the rule the people found when the Book of Moses was read aloud: no Ammonite or Moabite should ever enter the assembly of God (Nehemiah 13:1). Notice the word ever. The wording leaves no wiggle room. That one word covers a lot of ground.

Guard duty is a creative guess, baker, but the passage doesn't say it. The Book of Moses says no Ammonite or Moabite should ever enter the assembly of God (Nehemiah 13:1). Ever is the whole rule, and a guard post isn't part of it.

It's the other way around, friend. The text says they had not met the Israelites with food and water, but had hired a man named Balaam to call down a curse against them (Nehemiah 13:2). And the verse adds that our God had turned the curse into a blessing.

No seat at the table in this verse. Eliashib prepared a large room for Tobiah (Nehemiah 13:5). It was a room where they had previously stored the grain offerings, the frankincense, the temple articles, and the tithes.

False is right, baker. Nehemiah says that while all this was happening, he was not in Jerusalem, because he had returned to Artaxerxes king of Babylon (Nehemiah 13:6). So Eliashib's move happened while he was away. He discovered it after he obtained leave from the king to return to Jerusalem (Nehemiah 13:6-7).

Rent? It doesn't come up anywhere in this verse, friend. The text says Nehemiah was greatly displeased and threw all of Tobiah's household goods out of the room (Nehemiah 13:8). Greatly displeased is how he describes himself, and the goods went out.

True. After the purifying, Nehemiah had the articles of the house of God restored to the rooms, along with the grain offerings and frankincense (Nehemiah 13:9). First he ordered the rooms purified, then everything went back in. Moving day in reverse, and nobody had to rent a truck.
Tents sound reasonable, but the text says fields. The Levites and singers went back to their own fields (Nehemiah 13:10). Tents aren't mentioned anywhere in that verse.

False is right, baker! The text says he picked Shelemiah the priest, Zadok the scribe, Pedaiah of the Levites and Hanan to assist because they were considered trustworthy (Nehemiah 13:13). Trustworthy is the reason the verse gives. Nothing there says they were his relatives. I'd trust a team like that with my cookie boxes.
The nobles of Judah. Nehemiah rebukes them and asks, “What is this evil you are doing…” (Nehemiah 13:17). He goes right to the leaders. That takes nerve.

Babylon isn't in this verse, baker. Half of their children spoke the language of Ashdod or of the other peoples, but could not speak the language of Judah (Nehemiah 13:24). Babylon came up earlier, as where the king was.

Egypt doesn't show up in this verse, friend. The language these children can't speak is the language of Judah, and that's said of half of their children (Nehemiah 13:24). Those half speak the language of Ashdod or of the other peoples.

Sabbath trading was the earlier problem, handled with the gates and the warning (Nehemiah 13:19-21). This oath is about marriage. Nehemiah says, “You must not give your daughters in marriage to their sons…” (Nehemiah 13:25). Trading isn't part of it, baker.

Foreign! Nehemiah says, “Thus I purified the priests and Levites from everything foreign…” (Nehemiah 13:30). That's the word for the first blank. The second blank is about the duties he assigned to each of them.

Ancient sounds fitting for priests and Levites, but the text says he purified them from everything foreign (Nehemiah 13:30). That's the word the verse uses, baker. The second blank is about duties, since he assigned specific duties to each of them.
Wages aren't what he assigns here. The text says specific duties (Nehemiah 13:30). The Levites' earlier trouble was that their portions had not been given to them (Nehemiah 13:10), so I get the pull.
